name: Loja Highland Quichua
confidence_why: No source states a stress rule for Loja (Saraguro) Quichua itself: Orr (1978) only implies penultimate stress, through the Loja loan albúru 'árbol' restressed onto the penult and her remark that the penultimate syllable carries the prosodic accent so that only a displaced accent is written, Grimm (1896) gives penultimate stress as the ordinary pattern of Ecuadorian Quichua in general, and the modern Saraguro studies (Burneo 2016, Montaluisa 2019, Benalcázar 2020) say nothing about stress, so penultimate is the expected answer but it rests on indirect evidence.

catalog_quote: p. 23: "A menudo se altera la posición del acento a fin de adaptarse mejor a la estructura fonética del quichua, como en Azuay 'pájaro': pajáru. Otras veces se efectúa el cambio de una vocal, a fin de conformar la palabra el sistema fonético quichua, que tiene sólo tres vocales; por ejemplo, 'pensar': pinsana. El cambio de una consonante por otra, también es muy común; por ejemplo 'sábado': sabáru. A veces, se realiza una metátesis y se añade una vocal final, como en Loja: albúru 'árbol'." -- p. 10: "Obsérvese que la penúltima sílaba -na-, ejemplos 2 y 3, que tiene acento prosódico, pasa a ser parte de Pastaza y Tena, y el acento debe ser escrito. En el ejemplo 4, el acento se queda en la sílaba -nga-, aunque en Tena ha perdido la última sílaba, y debe ser escrito." -- Grimm 1896 §2 (general Ecuadorian Quichua, Loja not named): "Las palabras quichuas se acentúan ordinariamente en la penúltima sílaba."

new_statements.translation: p. 23: "The position of the accent is often altered so as to fit the phonetic structure of Quichua better, as in Azuay 'pájaro' [Sp. PÁjaro 'bird']: pajáru. [...] Sometimes a metathesis takes place and a final vowel is added, as in Loja: albúru 'árbol' [Sp. ÁRbol 'tree']." -- p. 10: "Note that the penultimate syllable -na-, examples 2 and 3, which carries the prosodic accent, becomes [final] in Pastaza and Tena, and the accent must be written. In example 4 the accent stays on the syllable -nga-, although in Tena it has lost the last syllable, and it must be written."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for loja1235, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict. This work supplies a first, weak indication of penultimate stress for Loja Quichua (one restressed loanword, albúru, plus the general Ecuadorian-Quichua convention that only non-penultimate stress is written). It should be entered as low-confidence, implicit evidence, not as a stated rule. The explicit stress remarks in the booklet concern the Oriente dialects Pastaza (qvz), Tena (quw) and Napo (qvo), not Loja.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The booklet never states a stress rule. It treats Ecuadorian Quichua as having penultimate word stress by default: the penult is the syllable 'que tiene acento prosódico', the practical orthography writes an accent only when stress ends up on the final syllable, and Spanish loans are restressed to the penult to fit 'la estructura fonética del quichua' (pajáru, sabáru). The single Loja datum is the loan albúru 'árbol' (Sp. árbol -> metathesis + added final vowel, stressed on the penult). So for Loja the evidence is one restressed loanword plus the general orthographic convention, not an explicit statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Only for the Oriente dialects, not Loja: in Pastaza and Tena the loss of a suffix consonant (locative -i, progressive -u-) 'hace que el acento caiga en la sílaba final' (p. 7); in Tena the truncated desiderative (rinaín, micunáin) and 3rd-person present verbs (pichán, shamún, micún) are stressed on the final syllable (p. 9); in the pretérito forms of Cuadro IV the stressed penult becomes final in Pastaza/Tena and the accent is then written (p. 10).
new_statements.identity_note: Orr 1978 treats 'Loja' as one of six Sierra provinces sampled (Imbabura, Pichincha, Tungurahua, Chimborazo, Azuay, Loja; p. 12) and names only the province, not the town; the Quichua-speaking area of Loja province is the Saraguro / San Lucas zone, i.e. loja1235. The booklet's explicit stress remarks (pp. 7-10) describe the Oriente dialects Pastaza, Tena and Napo (Northern Pastaza qvz, Tena Lowland quw, Napo Lowland qvo), not Loja; the p. 23 loanword remarks cover the Sierra dialects, with Azuay and Loja examples.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2.1 'Fonética de Saraguro' (pp. 40-49) gives vowel and consonant inventories of Saraguro Kichwa (communities Gera, Oñacapac, San Lucas) and sec. 5.1.1 compares Saraguro phonemes with unified Kichwa graphemes; there is no statement on stress/accent placement (the word 'tónica' appears once, p. 43, only as a positional criterion 'después de una sílaba tónica'; 'acento' never).

sources.note: Dialectological survey with Loja survey points (San Lucas, Saraguro) and a chapter reviewing prior dialect studies (Carpenter 1982 pp. 200-210, Lombeida-Naranjo 1976, Yánez, Stark 1985); segmental variation only. No statement on stress anywhere in the book (only 'acento' hit is about Parker's proto-Quechua 'acento de intensidad'). Notes (p. 201) that Consuelo Yánez did phonological studies of the Chimborazo, Imbabura and Loja dialects in the 1970s.
